query: For initially solid FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles exposed to the premelting and melting regime, the limited understanding of their thermal response prevents clear definition of their usable temperature range and behavior during high-temperature synthesis. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the onset and progression of their phase transition and why? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, relevant boundary conditions, supporting evidence from prior nanoparticle studies, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In solid FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles, the onset and progression of melting are governed by a size‐dependent surface energy effect coupled with thermally activated elemental segregation. In particular, lower-melting-point elements (such as Cu) preferentially migrate to the nanoparticle surfaces during heating, which lowers the local cohesive energy and thus initiates a surface premelting process. This molten surface layer then propagates inwards as the heating continues.
generation.material_initial_state: Initially solid, homogeneous, single-phase FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles (with controlled size distributions, e.g., ~5 nm and ~20 nm).
generation.intervention: Expose nanoparticles under inert atmosphere to a controlled heating ramp (e.g., via in situ TEM heating or DSC) while comparing two nanoparticle size ranges and, optionally, varying surface passivation (e.g., by adding or removing capping agents) to modulate surface mobility.
generation.conditions: Heating rates on the order of 5–10 K/min up to the melting regime, under inert (e.g., Ar) atmosphere; experiments carried out for nanoparticles with different diameters (e.g., small ~5 nm versus larger ~20 nm) and with/without surface modifiers.
generation.structural_mediator: Development of a surface layer enriched in a lower-melting component (e.g., Cu) that reduces the local melting point due to its lower cohesive energy and enhanced atomic mobility; the nanometer-scale high surface-to-volume ratio magnifies this effect.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures in the premelting regime, thermal energy induces differential atomic mobility. Lower-melting-point elements migrate to the nanoparticle surface, reducing the local melting point via a decrease in surface energy. This triggers an early onset of a disordered, quasi-liquid layer (premelting) at the surface that gradually propagates into the nanoparticle core as temperature increases.
generation.predicted_outcome: Smaller nanoparticles (with higher surface-to-volume ratios) and particles with undisturbed surface segregation will exhibit premelting at lower temperatures, evidenced by a detectable molten surface layer in in situ TEM and earlier endothermic features in DSC. Conversely, nanoparticles modified to inhibit surface segregation (e.g., via a strongly binding capping agent) will show a delayed premelting onset relative to the baseline.
generation.baseline: Homogeneous, chemically well-mixed solid nanoparticles with no pronounced surface segregation and typical DSC/TEM signatures of a sharp melting onset.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles in the 4–20 nm size range synthesized as fully solid precursors, under controlled inert-atmosphere heating conditions. It specifically addresses the premelting-to-melting transition regime, not the high-temperature liquid state.
generation.uncertainty: While prior thermal analyses (PMC7956699::web::009::3_results) and studies on disorder-to-order transitions in HEA nanoparticles (PMC8797181::web::000::abstract) suggest that nanoparticle size and surface energy critically influence phase transitions, the precise role and kinetics of surface elemental segregation in FeNiCrCoCu have not been directly observed. The new element in this proposal is the coupling of surface segregation with size effects to explain a gradual inward progression of melting, which remains uncertain until experimentally verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles differing primarily in size (e.g., 5 nm vs. 20 nm) and optionally in surface treatment (with and without a strongly binding capping agent). Subject the samples to controlled heating under inert atmosphere while monitoring in situ structural evolution using high-resolution TEM and simultaneously collecting DSC data.
measurements: In situ TEM observations to detect the onset and propagation of a disordered or molten surface layer.
DSC scans to record endothermic peaks corresponding to premelting/melting events.
Elemental mapping (e.g., via EDS in TEM) to monitor any surface enrichment of Cu or other elements.
Comparative analysis of heating curves between size and surface-treated groups.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no significant difference in the premelting onset temperature, the spatial progression of melting (i.e., absence of a distinct molten surface layer), or the expected elemental segregation pattern is observed between the nanoparticles of different sizes (or between surface-modified and unmodified particles), then the hypothesis that size and surface segregation govern the melting onset will be falsified.

Nanoscale multi-principal element intermetallics (MPEIs) may provide a broad and tunable compositional space of active, high–surface area materials with potential applications such as catalysis and magnetics. However, MPEI nanoparticles are challenging to fabricate because of the tendency of the particles to grow/agglomerate or phase-separated during annealing. Here, we demonstrate a disorder-to-order phase transition approach that enables the synthesis of ultrasmall (4 to 5 nm) and stable MPEI nanoparticles (up to eight elements). We apply just 5 min of Joule heating to promote the phase transition of the nanoparticles into L10 intermetallic structure, which is then preserved by rapidly cooling. This disorder-to-order transition results in phase-stable nanoscale MPEIs with compositions (e.g., PtPdAuFeCoNiCuSn), which have not been previously attained by traditional synthetic methods. This synthesis strategy offers a new paradigm for developing previously unexplored MPEI nanoparticles by accessing a nanoscale-size regime and novel compositions with potentially broad applications. Multi-principal element intermetallic nanoparticles are synthesized via disorder-to-order transition.
